claims.case_section: Evaluating the Workshop Pronunciation & Origin Hypothesis
claims.short_label: 1828–1901 survey of 14 dictionary editions documents Merriam-Webster hard /g/ on 'gimmal' and 'gimmer'
claims.statement: A systematic survey of 14 major British and American dictionary editions from 1828 to 1901 (orthoepic_dictionary_survey_1828_1901) demonstrates that Noah Webster (1828) and the entire nineteenth-century Springfield Merriam-Webster lineage through Webster's International Dictionary (1890), along with the Imperial Dictionary (1882) and Funk & Wagnalls's Standard Dictionary (1893), explicitly prescribed hard velar /g/ ('Ḡĭm\'mal', 'Ḡĭm\'mer') on the mechanical 'hinge/interlocking ring' word family—contrasting with /dʒ/ in Worcester (1846, 1860), the Century Dictionary (1889), and OED1 (1901).
claims.rationale: Modern dismissals of Eric Partridge's gimbal/gimcrack connection often assume that 'gimmal'/'gimbal' and 'gimmer' always had soft /dʒ/ in nineteenth-century American English. Primary-scan diacritical inspection proves that New England's dominant school and shop authority (Merriam-Webster, 1828–1890) consistently marked initial hard /g/ with a macron ('Ḡ') on 'gimmal' and 'gimmer', matching hard-/g/ 'gimcrack'.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Explicit nineteenth-century lexicographical prescription of hard velar /g/ for mechanical 'gimmal' and 'gimmer' across all surveyed Merriam-Webster editions (1828–1890), Ogilvie/Annandale (1882), and Funk & Wagnalls (1893).
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Unmediated vernacular pronunciation among unlettered New England mechanics or the morphological derivation of 'gimmick' itself (evaluated separately in CLM-1100-011).
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: How widely spoken New England shop usage followed Merriam-Webster's hard-/g/ prescription versus Worcester/Century's soft-/dʒ/ norm.

limitations: Dictionary pronunciation keys document prescriptive orthoepic norms rather than direct phonetic transcriptions of working-class shop speech.

evidence.reason: Noah Webster's 1828 American Dictionary Vol. I prescribing unmarked hard G on 'GIM\'MAL' and 'GIM\'MER'.
evidence.witness_note: Anchors the 14-edition orthoepic_dictionary_survey_1828_1901 block in gimmick.json (WEBSTER-1828-1ED through OED1-BRADLEY-1901).

evidence.reason: Webster's International Dictionary (1890, p. 624) printing explicit macron-G ('Ḡĭm\'mal', 'Ḡĭm\'mer' = /g/).
Ogilvie & Annandale's Imperial Dictionary (1882, Vol. II, p. 406) respelling '(gim\'al)' and '(gim\'ėr)' with hard /g/.
1865 Webster-Mahn dictionary plate confirming matching initial hard /g/ on mechanical 'Gim\'crack'.
OED1 (1901, Henry Bradley) s.v. gimmer ('hinge, mechanical catch'), representing the competing British /dʒ/ orthoepic tradition.

claims.target_lexeme: gimmick, n. (< mechanical gimmer / gimmal / gimlick / gimcrack)
claims.case_section: Evaluating the Workshop Pronunciation & Origin Hypothesis
claims.short_label: Partially supported domestic workshop derivation from hard-/g/ 'gimmer'/'gimmal'/'gimlick' + '-ick' (± 'gimcrack')
claims.statement: Phonological alignment (hard /g/ prescribed in Merriam-Webster on 'gimmal'/'gimmer' and 'gimcrack'), morphological parallels (New England dialect 'gimlick' for 'gimlet' in 1825 and unstressed '-ock -> -ick' reduction in 'bastick, maddick, mammick'), and referent alignment (hinged/pivoted eccentric 'come-along' jaws in 1897 Boston) partially support deriving 'gimmick' domestically within the English 'gim-' mechanical-hinge/contrivance family, while pre-1893 transitional workshop forms remain unattested.
claims.rationale: Unlike foreign-loan proposals that conflict in stress, vowel quality, and semantics, the domestic English 'gim-' mechanical cluster shares initial stress, hard /g/ in New England's standard dictionary tradition, diminutive/tool '-ick' remodeling, and the exact 'hinged mechanical catch / trivial mechanism' semantics seen in 1893 Maine and 1897 Boston—while rigorous checking excludes Shropshire 'ferrick' (< 'ferry', not 'ferrule') and unattested '*gimmock' from serving as direct intermediate proofs.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Phonological, morphological, and semantic plausibility of a nineteenth-century New England workshop formation or blend within the hard-/g/ 'gimmer/gimmal/gimlick/gimcrack' family.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: A closed etymological proof, since no pre-1893 text yet attests '*gimmock' or explicitly glosses 'gimmick' as a variant of 'gimmer' or 'gimcrack'.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: Whether 'gimmick' arose via suffixal remodeling of 'gimmer'/'gimmal' on tool nouns in '-ick' ('gimlick'), expressive blending of 'gimcrack' with 'nick'/'trick'/'flick', or independent workshop sound symbolism.

limitations: Wright's English Dialect Dictionary (1900, CERT-900-305) records zero tokens of '*gimmock', and Jackson's Shropshire Word-Book (1881, CERT-1100-305) shows 'ferrick' derives from 'ferry' rather than 'ferrule'.
resolution_criteria: Locate a pre-1893 New England machine-shop, textile-mill, telegraph, or hardware text attesting a transitional form or explicitly linking 'gimmick' with 'gimmer', 'gimmal', 'gimlick', or 'gimcrack'.
Locate nineteenth-century New England dialect fieldwork documenting spoken hard-/g/ 'gimmer' ('hinged catch or clamp') among mechanics or linemen.

claims.target_lexeme: gimmick (vs. German Gemach and Dutch gemak)
claims.case_section: Evaluating the Workshop Pronunciation & Origin Hypothesis
claims.short_label: Phonological stress and 'comfort/apartment/privy' semantics weigh against German Gemach and Dutch gemak
claims.statement: Primary German and Dutch lexicographical records weigh strongly against deriving 'gimmick' from German Gemach (/ɡəˈmax/) or Dutch gemak (/ɣəˈmɑk/), both of which bear final-syllable stress with open /a/ and denote 'ease, comfort, room, privy' rather than a small mechanical tool or catch.
claims.rationale: Inspection of Grimm's Deutsches Wörterbuch (1884, CERT-900-306) and Sewel's Dutch-English dictionary (1766, CERT-900-308) confirms acute prosodic mismatch (iambic /ɡəˈmax/ vs. trochaic /ˈɡɪmɪk/), vocalic mismatch (/a/ vs. /ɪ/), semantic mismatch ('convenience, apartment, house of office'), and absence of German/Dutch demographic framing in 1893 Bucksport, Maine or 1897 Boston transit inventories.

evidence_boundary.establishes: Severe prosodic, vocalic, semantic, and geographic mismatches weighing against German Gemach and Dutch gemak as primary donors of 'gimmick'.
evidence_boundary.does_not_establish: Absolute impossibility of secondary bilingual punning once 'gimmick' later spread to the Midwest.
evidence_boundary.remaining_uncertainty: None within nineteenth-century German and Dutch standard lexicography.

limitations: Evaluates published scholarly donor suggestions on phonological and semantic grounds rather than labeling them folk myths.

evidence.reason: Grimm's Deutsches Wörterbuch (1884) s.v. Gemach, documenting final stress and 'rest, comfort, room, privy' senses without 'small tool/clamp'.
Sewel's 1766 Groot Woordenboek s.v. gemak ('ease, conveniency, house of office'), lacking mechanical-tool semantics.
